You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in the orthorhombic space group Fmmm (No. 69, Hall symbol −F 2 2), but the supplied atomic coordinates refer to a nonstandard twelve-atom input cell rather than to the conventional face-centered cell. The input lattice has parameters a = 8.6196034 Å, b = 8.54422596 Å, c = 6.13399826 Å, with interaxial angles α = 69.71970416°, β = 68.40450351°, and γ = 41.87579233°. This cell contains four europium, two zinc, and six germanium atoms, giving the input composition Eu₄Zn₂Ge₆. Because the input frame is not the standard Fmmm frame, the fractional coordinates q in the two settings are related by q_standard = P q_input + s, where P has rows (approximately 0, −1/2, −1/2), (−1/2, approximately 0, −1/2), and (1/2, 1/2, approximately 0), with the tiny off-diagonal and diagonal entries of order 10⁻¹⁷ reflecting numerical rounding, and the origin shift s is (0, 0, 0) to within the same numerical precision. All coordinate values below are given in the standard Fmmm frame and are rounded to six decimal places.

In the standard face-centered orthorhombic setting, the europium atoms occupy two independent eightfold orbits. The first europium orbit is the Wyckoff position 8h, with coordinate relation (0, y, 0) and representative site (0, 0.244632, 0); the single free parameter is y = 0.244632, and the F-centered symmetry generates eight equivalent europium positions per conventional cell. The second europium orbit is the fixed Wyckoff position 8f at (1/4, 1/4, 1/4), which has no free positional parameter and likewise contributes eight europium atoms through the face-centering and mirror symmetries.

Zinc occupies a single independent orbit, the Wyckoff position 8i with coordinate relation (0, 0, z). Its representative atom lies at (0, 0, 0.333537), so the only free coordinate is z = 0.333537; the symmetry operations of Fmmm expand this site into eight equivalent zinc positions.

Germanium is distributed over two independent sublattices. The first is another 8i orbit of the form (0, 0, z), with representative position (0, 0, 0.168889) and free parameter z = 0.168889, giving eight symmetry-related germanium atoms along this axial family. The second germanium sublattice is the sixteenfold Wyckoff position 16n, described by the coordinate relation (x, 0, z). Its representative site is (0.246035, 0, 0.415672), with independent parameters x = 0.246035 and z = 0.415672; the full Fmmm symmetry generates sixteen equivalent germanium atoms from this orbit.

Taken together, the conventional Fmmm cell therefore contains two crystallographically distinct europium sublattices at (0, 0.244632, 0) and (1/4, 1/4, 1/4), one zinc sublattice at (0, 0, 0.333537), and two germanium sublattices at (0, 0, 0.168889) and (0.246035, 0, 0.415672). No positional corrections beyond the stated six-decimal rounding are required, so these coordinates represent the input geometry directly.
